The present appeal has been filed by the appellant/convict under Section 374 (3) Cr.P.C. against the judgment of conviction dated 11.03.2020 and order on sentence dated 12.09.2022 passed by Ld.
MM, North, Rohini Courts thereby convicting the appellant/convict as follows:
(i) Simple Imprisonment for a period of one month for the offence punishable under Section 279 IPC.
(ii) Simple Imprisonment for a period of one month for the offence punishable under Section 337 IPC.
(iii) Simple Imprisonment for a period of two months for the offence punishable under Section 338 IPC.
(iv) Simple Imprisonment for a period of three months for the offence punishable under Section 304A IPC.
(v) Simple Imprisonment for a period of nine months and fine of Rs.10,000/- for the offence punishable under Section 471 IPC.

In default of payment of fine, to undergo Mohan Singh vs The State on 18 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49985869/
1 further simple imprisonment for a period of one month.
2. Brief facts of the case are that on 16.03.2011 at 11.00 a.m at Sector 3-4 dividing road near NDPL Office, DSIDC Bawana, Delhi, accused Mohan Singh (appellant herein) was found driving a vehicle Mahinidra Champion bearing no. DL- 1LL-8207 in rash and negligent manner and while driving in such manner and taking a turn near Sector 3, the above said vehicle turned upside down as a result of which the passengers Sinto, Pintoo and Gulab sustained simple injuries and Raj Nath suffered grievous injuries suffered by him.

CHARGE 3.

Vide order dated 24.09.2013, notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was served upon the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 279/337/338/304A/471 IPC to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
Thereafter, the matter was fixed for prosecution evidence and in order to prove its case, the prosecution has examined 12 witnesses.

EVIDENCE 4. PW-1 Sh. Sinto deposed that on the day of incident at about 10.00 a.m. he was present in the factory with his brother and one three wheeler came in the factory after which two compressors were loaded in the tempo and he along with his brother sat in the tempo.
He further deposed that the vehicle was driven by accused very speedily and in a negligent manner and as a result of that, it met with an accident and his brother died in the accident.
He has identified the accused and the offending vehicle in the court.

PW-2 Gulab and PW-3 Pintoo narrated the whole incident to the police as deposed by PW1 and PW2 Gulab furtehr proved the arrest memo of accused Ex.PW2/A and identified the seizure memo Ex.PW2/B of the driving licence of the accused.

PW-4 Rahul Kakkar deposed that he was the owner of the offending vehicle bearing no.
DL-1LL-8207 and he replied to the notice under Section 133 MV Act Ex.PW4/A and has produced the offending vehicle Ex.P1 in the court.

PW-4 Shiv Kumar (wrongly mentioned as PW4) deposed that he went to BSA Hospital and identified the dead body of his younger brother Jhuru Lal vide identification memo and handing over memo Ex.PW4/A and Ex.PW4/B respectively.
PW-5 Raj Nath deposed on the same lines as PW1 and identified the accused.

PW-6 Ct. Vikram deposed that on 16.03.2011 he was posted at PS Bawana and he along with HC Joginder Singh went to the spot i.e. 3-4 crossing near NDPL Office and at the spot, they found offending vehicle bearing no. DL-1LL-8207 in turtled condition after which HC Joginder went to the hospital and he remained at the spot and HC Joginder prepared the rukka and handed over to him Mohan Singh vs The State on 18 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49985869/
2 for registration of FIR and HC Joginder clicked the photographs of the spot after which the IO seized the offending vehicle vide seizure memo Ex.PW6/A.
He has also identified the photographs of the offending vehicle on the spot as Ex.P1 to P3 and P3 (colly).

PW-7 SI Deepk Purohit deposed that on 23.03.2011 he received DD No. 28B after which he went to the hospital and got preserved the dead body of deceased and on 24.03.2011, he prepared inquest report and recorded the statement of relatives of deceased Ex.PW7/A and Ex.PW4/A and the inquest papers were proved as Ex.PW7/B and handing over memo of dead body as Ex.PW7/D.

PW8 Retd. SI Rajender deposed that on 08.04.2011 he received the present case file and he obtained the opinion on MLC of Raj Nath Singh and sent the DL of accused for verification and the verification form was proved as Ex.PW8/A.
He further deposed that he recorded the disclosure statement of accused as Ex.PW8/B and also arrested the accused and conducted his personal search vide memos Ex.PW8/C and Ex.PW8/D respectively.
PW-9 Retd.
ASI/Technician Devender Kumar deposed that on 19.03.2011 he conducted the mechanical inspection of offending vehicle bearing no. DL-1LL-8207 and proved the detailed report as Ex.PW9/A.

PW-10 ASI Joginder deposed that on 16.03.2011 he was posted at PS Bawana and he received DD No.16A after which he went to the spot i.e. 3-4 crossing near NDPL office and at the spot, they found offending vehicle bearing no. DL-1LL- 8207 in over turned condition and he clicked the photographs of the vehicle and he went to the hospital and collected the MLC of the injured persons and also prepared rukka Ex.PW10/B at the spot and seized the offending vehicle.

He further deposed that he sent the notice under Section 133 M.V. Act on 17.03.2011 and prepared the site plan Ex.PW10/D and arrested accused, conducted his personal search Ex.PW10/E and also seized the documents of the offending vehicles.

PW-11 Ct. Surender deposed that on 26.05.2011 he went to the transport authority Kolkatta and got verified the driving licencne of the the accused which was foundn to be fake and not issued from the office.
5. During the course of evidence, statement of accused was recorded under Section 294 Cr.P.C.

where he did not dispute the identity of certain documents and admitted the following documents:
(i) MLCs 1003/11, 1004/11, 1005/11, 1006/11 & 1007/11 as Ex.A1 to Ex.A5.
(ii) X-ray report of Rajnath as Ex.A6.

(iii)Death report no. 98452 as Ex.A7.
(iv)PM report no. 43/11 as Ex.A8.

(v) FIR No. 95/11 and DD No.16A as Ex.A9 & A10.
6.
After closure of prosecution evidence, statement of accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C was recorded on 27.02.2020 in which appellant pleads innocence and false implication.

7. I have heard Mr. Ranjeet Kumar, ld. Counsel for the appellant/convict and Ld. Addl. PP for the State and perused the record carefully.
GROUNDS OF APPEAL 8.

Aggrieved by the judgment of conviction dated 11.03.2020 and order on sentence dated 12.09.2022 passed by Ld. MM, North, Rohini Courts, the present appeal has been preferred on the ground that the said judgment has been passed in mechanical manner.

It is stated that the findings of the Ld. Trial Court are contrary to the record and the facts / evidence placed on the record does not warrant conviction, as there are number of contradictions in the testimonies of the material witnesses.
Therefore, it is prayed that the judgment of conviction and order on sentence are liable to be set aside and appellant is liable to be acquitted.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Addl. PP for the State has strongly controverted the above arguments of the Ld. Counsel for the appellant/convict and has argued that there is no illegality or infirmity in the judgment under challenge, which has been passed after considering all the evidence on the record.
10. Heard.
Trial Court Record perused.
FINDINGS 11.
The ld. Trial court vide judgment dated 11.03.2020 observed that case of the prosecution has been proved.

12. It was incumbent upon the prosecution to prove the following ingredients to establish the guilt of the accused under Section 279 and 304A IPC:
(i) The accused was driving his vehicle on a public way and caused the accident.
(ii) It must have been caused by rash or negligent act/driving of the accused.
( iii )
The death so caused, must be causa causans of the rash and negligent act/driving of the accused.

13. To impose criminal liability under this Section, it is necessary that the death should have been the direct result of a rash and negligent act of the accused and that act must be proximate cause without the intervention of another's negligence.

It must be the causa causans: it is not enough that it may have been the causa sine qua non.
14.
Rash or negligent act is an act done and intentionally or designedly.

A rash act is primarily an over hasty act and is thus opposed to a deliberate act but it also includes an act which, though it may be said to be deliberate is yet done without due deliberation and caution.

Negligence is the breach of Mohan Singh vs The State on 18 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49985869/
4 a duty caused by omission to do something which a reasonable man guided by those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or the doing of something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do.

sentences.text: Negligence is the genus of which rashness is a specie.

In order that rashness or negligence may be criminal, it must be of such a degree as to amount to taking hazard knowing that the hazard was of such a degree that injury was most likely to be caused thereby.
The criminality lies in running the risk or doing such an act, with recklessness and indifference to the consequences.

Hon'ble Supreme court of India in Baba Chandra Vs. State of Maharashtra 1968 SC 1319 held that:
"Criminal negligence is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge has arisen, it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted.''
9.

sentences.text:
Culpable rashness is acting with consciousness that the mischievous and illegal consequences may follow, but with the hope that FIR No.648/95 5/10 they will not,
and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precaution to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite the consciousness."
15. I have carefully perused the testimony of PW1, PW2, PW3 and PW5 the complainant, who were the star prosecution witnesses.

Vide their testimonies, they have proved the presence of accused and the factum of accident taking place on 16.03.2011, wherein Sinto, Pintoo, and Gulab sustained simple injuries and Raj Nath sustained grievous injuries and the deceased Jhuru was fatally injured.
The factum of accident has not been disputed by the accused even in his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
Even the identity of the offending vehicle has not been disputed by the accused.

The death of the deceased Jhuru having been cause as a result of road accident, also stands proved by the postmortem report proved as Ex.A8, wherein it had been opined that the death was due to craniocerebral damage consequent to blunt force impact to head possible in a road traffic accident.
The testimony of PW1 was duly corroborated with the testimony of PW2, PW3 and PW5.
The testimony of PW1, who was with the deceased at the time of incident does not suffer from any infirmity and is found to be trustworthy and natural.
It was argued by ld. Counsel for the appellant that merely driving at a high speed would not amount to a rash or negligent driving.
The accused being the driver of the offending vehicle is again not disputed.
16. Thus, after perusal of the record and the findings given, there is no illegality in the judgment dated 11.03.2020 and the ld.
Trial court has thus rightly convicted the accused for the offence punishable under Section 279/337/338/304A/471 IPC and the judgment dated 11.03.2020 is upheld.

The Court is mindful of the sentencing policy and its impact on all the stakeholders.
"......The law regulates social interests, arbitrates conflicting claims an demands.
Security of persons and property of the people is an essential function of the State.
It could be achieved through instrumentality of criminal law.
Undoubtedly, there is a cross cultural conflict where living law must find answer to the new challenges and the courts are required to mould the sentencing system to meet the challenges.
The contagion of lawlessness would undermine social order and lay it in ruins.
Protection of society and stamping out criminal proclivity must be the object of law which must be achieved by imposing appropriate sentence.

Therefore, law as a corner-stone of the edifice of "order"
should meet the challenges confronting the society.

Friedman in his "Law in Changing Society"
stated that, "State of criminal law continues to be - as it should be - a decisive reflection of social consciousness of society".
Therefore, in operating the sentencing system, law should adopt the corrective machinery or the deterrence based on factual matrix.
By deft modulation sentencing process be stern where it should be, and tempered with mercy where it warrants to be.

The facts and given circumstances in each case, the nature of the crime, the manner in which it was planned and committed, the motive for commission of the crime, the conduct of the accused, the nature of weapons used and all other attending circumstances are relevant facts which would enter into the area of consideration.

Therefore, undue sympathy to impose inadequate sentence would do more harm to the justice system to undermine the public confidence in the efficacy of law and society could not long endure under such serious threats.
It is, therefore, the duty of every court to award proper sentence having regard to the nature of the offence and the manner in which it was executed or committed etc.
This position was illuminatingly stated by this Court in Sevaka Perumal etc. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1991 (3) SCC 471).

entities.text: Sevaka Perumal etc. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1991 (3) SCC 471)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The criminal law adheres in general to the principle of proportionality in prescribing liability according to the culpability of each kind of criminal conduct.

It ordinarily allows some significant discretion to the Judge in arriving at a sentence in each case, presumably to permit sentences that reflect more subtle considerations of culpability that are raised by the special facts of each case.
Judges in essence affirm that punishment ought always to fit the crime; yet in practice sentences are determined largely by other considerations.
Sometimes it is the correctional needs of the perpetrator that are offered to justify a sentence.

Sometimes the desirability of keeping him out of circulation,
and sometimes even the tragic results of his crime.
Inevitably these considerations cause a departure from just desert as the basis of punishment and create cases of apparent injustice that are serious and widespread.
Proportion between crime and punishment is a goal respected in principle, and in spite of errant notions, it remains a strong influence in the determination of sentences.

The practice of punishing all serious crimes with equal severity is now unknown in civilized societies, but such a radical departure from the principle of proportionality has disappeared from the law only in recent times.

6
Even now for a single grave infraction drastic sentences are imposed.
Anything less than a penalty of greatest severity for any serious crime is thought then to be a measure of toleration that is unwarranted and unwise.

But in fact, quite apart from those considerations that make punishment unjustifiable when it is out of proportion to the crime, uniformly disproportionate punishment has some very undesirable practical consequences."
18. Reliance is placed upon Shailesh Jasvantbhai & Anr vs State Of Gujarat & Ors Appeal (Crl.) 118 of 2006 DOD by Supreme Court, 19 January, 2006.

sentences.text: 19. The appellant has been convicted to undergo (I) Simple Imprisonment for a period of one month for the offence punishable under Section 279 IPC, (ii) Simple Imprisonment for a period of one month for the offence punishable under Section 337 IPC, (iii) Simple Imprisonment for a period of two months for the offence punishable under Section 338 IPC, (iv) Simple Imprisonment for a period of three months for the offence punishable under Section 304A IPC and (v) Simple Imprisonment for a period of nine months and fine of Rs.10,000/- for the offence punishable under Section 471 IPC.
In default of payment of fine, to undergo further simple imprisonment for a period of one month.
20. Normally the Appellate Court would not interfere in the discretion exercised by the Ld. Trial Court in awarding the sentence or fine.

However, in the interest of justice, since the matter pertains to the year 2011 and convict has already undergone trial for a considerable time of almost 12 years,
there is no other previous involvement of the convict which has been brought to the knowledge of the court and accordingly as per Section 386(b) (iii) Cr.P.C. without altering the finding given by the ld. Trial court, the sentence is altered to the extent that the appellant Mohan Singh be sentenced for imprisonment for the period already undergone and fine of Rs.10,000/-.
Fine paid.
Receipt issued.
Order on sentence passed by ld. Trial Court dated 12.09.2022 is modified to this extent.
(It is pertinent to mention that as per the finding of the ld. Trial Court, the victim's family was not traceable.
Therefore, compensation is not being awarded, however, they shall be at liberty to claim compensation in accordance with law and subsisting rules under the Victim Compensation Scheme).
21. In view of the above discussion, the appeal is disposed off accordingly.
22. TCR, if any be sent back to the concerned court with copy of this order.
23. Appeal files be consigned to record room.
